title: Smartwatch alert for an irregular rate above 180 bpm leads to a ventricular tachycardia diagnosis, an ICD, and the incidental discovery and resection of a lung adenocarcinoma
summary: A 58-year-old's smartwatch flagged an irregular rate over 180 bpm; NSVT was diagnosed from watch data, an ICD placed, and the post-procedure X-ray found a 28 mm lung adenocarcinoma, resected.
account: Cole, Kar, Nimako and Smelt, of St George's Healthcare NHS Trust (thoracic surgery) and East Surrey Hospital (respiratory medicine) in England, reported in JRSM Open (published 4 January 2022; the event dates are not given, so the publication date is used) a previously well 58-year-old non-smoker whose smartwatch alerted him that his heart rate was irregular and exceeding 180 beats per minute while he felt nothing. His GP's 12-lead ECG showed tachycardia without arrhythmia and he was admitted; inpatient ECGs showed incomplete right bundle branch block and intermittent first-degree AV block but captured no significant arrhythmia. Using the smartwatch results, the cardiologist diagnosed non-sustained ventricular tachycardia and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator was inserted. The post-procedure chest X-ray, taken to exclude pneumothorax, incidentally showed a right upper zone abnormality; CT found a 28 mm lesion, PET showed FDG-avid nodes, and biopsy showed lepidic adenocarcinoma, staged cT1c N0 M0. He underwent a video-assisted right upper lobectomy with node dissection, was discharged on day 10, and the 35 mm tumor was staged pT2a pN0 M0 with clear margins; the nodes showed sarcoidosis and cardiac MRI found no cardiac sarcoid. The authors call this the first reported case of a smartwatch assisting the diagnosis of both NSVT and lung adenocarcinoma. The watch's brand and model are not stated.
purpose: The watch's heart-rate alert was its intended function; the lung cancer diagnosis was an incidental consequence of the ICD procedure that the alert set in motion, outside anything the device was built to do.
system: Smartwatch heart-rate and irregular-rhythm alert (brand and model not stated)
developer: Not stated (the report does not name the device's maker)
location: United Kingdom (authors at St George's Healthcare NHS Trust, London, and East Surrey Hospital, Redhill; the treating hospitals are not named)
taxonomy_note: No health category exists; Accessibility is used because consumer monitoring outside the clinic caught an asymptomatic arrhythmia that inpatient ECGs did not. The second benefit (early-stage lung cancer resected) is incidental, which is why 'unexpected' is true. Brand unstated in the full text ('apple' appears only in a reference title), as the earlier verifier noted.

ratings.reason: One man received an ICD for ventricular tachycardia and curative resection of a lung adenocarcinoma found at stage pT2a pN0; the authors judge that without the watch the cancer would likely have grown undetected and curative surgery might not have been an option, a counterfactual that is their judgment.

ai_role.statement: The watch's alert in an asymptomatic man started the chain, and its stored data were what the cardiologist used to diagnose NSVT when hospital tracings captured nothing; the lung cancer was found by a routine post-ICD X-ray, not by the device. The brand is unknown, so the alerting algorithm cannot be identified; the authors describe smartwatch rhythm monitoring generically as photoplethysmography.

produced_by: An asymptomatic wearer whose smartwatch alerted to an irregular rate above 180 bpm and who took it to his GP
A cardiologist willing to diagnose from the watch's stored data when hospital tracings were silent
A procedure (ICD insertion) whose routine follow-up imaging happened to cover the lung
must_hold: The arrhythmia is one the watch records while hospital monitoring misses it
The incidental finding is in the field of the post-procedure X-ray and is caught early enough for curative surgery; the authors cite an estimated 1 in 25 cancers diagnosed incidentally
